mainTopic: התפסה in נדרים according to רבא, and רבי יוחנן's split between שבועת שקר and שבועת שוא
overview: The amud opens with a challenge to רבא, who holds that attaching to an oath (מתפיס בשבועה) does not count as an oath. רבא answers by rereading the ברייתא so that it speaks only about vows (נדרים), and שמואל adds that the earlier vow must really exist. A פסוק, 'אִישׁ כִּי יִדֹּר נֶדֶר', shows that התפסה belongs only to vows. The גמרא then explains that the ברייתא's real new point is the day גדליה בן אחיקם was killed: a vow still takes hold even on a public fast day. Next, רבין reports that רבי יוחנן agrees with רבא. A second teaching of רבי יוחנן, brought by רב דימי, says a broken oath about the future is שקר and a false oath about the past is שוא, each with its own לאו, and that breaking קונמות transgresses 'לא יחל דברו'. A ברייתא that calls שוא and שקר 'one' is explained to mean they were said in a single utterance, like זכור and שמור. That link teaches that שוא gets lashes just like שקר. The גמרא then asks why this is not obvious and begins an answer from רב פפא, which continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The ברייתא Seems to Contradict רבא
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא points out that the ברייתא, as just read, causes a problem for רבא.
steps.simpleTranslation: But according to רבא, this is difficult!
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא we just learned seemed to back up אביי. So the גמרא says that רבא now has a problem.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא appeared to treat attaching (התפסה) as a real binding act, which fits אביי's view that מתפיס בשבועה counts as an oath. רבא holds that attaching to an oath does not work, so the ברייתא seems to go against him. The next step gives רבא's answer.

keyTerms.meaning: It is difficult; a challenge to someone's view
But; here it turns the question onto the other opinion

phrases.english: But according to רבא, it is difficult!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns the ברייתא, which had seemed to help אביי, into a challenge against רבא.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's view that attaching to an oath (מתפיס בשבועה) is not an oath.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא appears to treat attaching as binding, against רבא.

steps.title: רבא Rereads the ברייתא as Talking About Vows
steps.stepSummary: רבא changes the reading of the ברייתא so that it talks about the 'bond of a vow'. That way it only teaches that attaching works for נדרים. שמואל adds that the earlier vow must really exist.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא could answer you: Fix the wording and read it like this. What is the 'bond of a vow' that the תורה speaks about? It is someone who says, 'It is upon me not to eat meat and not to drink wine, like the day my father died,' or 'like the day so-and-so was killed.' And שמואל said: This works only if he is already under a vow from that day.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא answers the challenge by reading the ברייתא so that it is about vows (נדרים), not oaths. שמואל then adds a condition about when this attaching works.
steps.deeperAnalysis: By adding the word 'נדר', רבא limits the ברייתא to vows. Attaching a new prohibition to an existing one works for נדרים, which says nothing about שבועות. שמואל's condition means the person must really have an existing vow from that day, such as a vow never to eat meat on the day his father died. Only then is there a real vow to attach to.

keyTerms.meaning: Fix the wording and read it this way
A 'bond': a prohibition a person puts on himself (from the פסוק in במדבר)
A vow, which forbids an object on a person
Already under a vow from before
So-and-so; an unnamed person

steps.confusionAlert: Don't think the person is simply copying a sad day by choice. According to שמואל, the attaching only works if he already has a real vow in place for that day.

phrases.english: רבא could say to you:
Fix it and say it like this:
Which is the bond of a vow mentioned in the Torah?
One who says: "It is upon me

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁלֹּא אוֹכַל בָּשָׂר וְשֶׁלֹּא אֶשְׁתֶּה יַיִן״
phrases.english: that I will not eat meat and that I will not drink wine"
like the day on which his father died,
like the day on which so-and-so was killed.
And שמואל said:
And that is only when he has been under a vow from that day on.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לָךְ רָבָא, תָּרֵיץ וְאֵימָא הָכִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge against רבא by rereading the ברייתא.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rereading the text: the ברייתא is limited to vows.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא teaches that attaching works in general, including oaths, as אביי says.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא only teaches that attaching works for vows. It says nothing about oaths, so רבא stands.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up the main line of the sugya: התפסה is a rule that belongs to נדרים only.

steps.title: Why Must There Be an Existing Vow?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the source of שמואל's condition.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why שמואל requires that the person already be under a vow. This question sets up the next step, which brings a פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שמואל's condition needs a source. Without one, we might think attaching to any prohibition works, even one that came from somewhere other than a vow.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the reason?

phrases.english: What is the reason?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the source of שמואל's condition.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The source showing that one can only attach to something forbidden by a vow.

steps.title: The Verse: Vowing by Something Already Vowed
steps.stepSummary: The פסוק 'אִישׁ כִּי יִדֹּר נֶדֶר' teaches that attaching works only to something that is itself forbidden by a vow.
steps.simpleTranslation: The פסוק says: 'When a man vows a vow to ה'.' This means it only works when he vows by attaching to something that is forbidden by a vow.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers with a פסוק. The doubled wording 'vows a vow' teaches that a person can attach only to an existing vow.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Because the source for attaching speaks about vows, attaching is limited to vows in two ways. The thing you attach to must be forbidden by a vow, and the rule applies to נדרים and not to שבועות. This supports רבא's position.

keyTerms.meaning: He vows a vow; the doubled wording teaches the rule
Something forbidden through a vow

steps.whatToRemember: התפסה works only when you attach to something forbidden by a נדר, and only in the world of vows. That is why רבא can say it does not work for oaths.

phrases.english: The verse states:
"When a man vows a vow to the Lord"
only when he vows by something that is forbidden by a vow.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר קְרָא: אִישׁ כִּי יִדֹּר נֶדֶר לַה׳
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question by bringing a פסוק.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The doubled wording 'יִדֹּר נֶדֶר' teaches that one must attach to something forbidden by a vow.

steps.title: Isn't the Father's Day Case Obvious?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the ברייתא's first example and asks why it needed to be said at all.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Like the day his father died.' That is obvious!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the example from the ברייתא and challenges it as too obvious to need teaching.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A vow not to eat meat on the day one's father died is a plain, voluntary vow. So it is clear that a new vow can be attached to it. Why would the ברייתא bother to state such a simple case?

keyTerms.meaning: It is obvious! Why say it?

phrases.english: "Like the day on which his father died."
That is obvious!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the source of the rule to analyzing the wording of the ברייתא.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's need to mention the example of his father's death day.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A voluntary vow is clearly a real vow, so teaching that one can attach to it seems unnecessary.

steps.title: The Real Point: The Day Gedaliah Was Killed
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא needed the second example, the day גדליה בן אחיקם was killed (a public fast day). Otherwise we might think a vow cannot take hold on a day that is already forbidden anyway.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was needed for the case of 'like the day גדליה בן אחיקם was killed.' You might have thought: since meat and wine are forbidden that day even without a vow, his vow does not create a prohibition, so this would not count as attaching to a vow. So the ברייתא teaches us otherwise.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the important example is the second one, the 'פלוני' who was killed, meaning גדליה בן אחיקם. The ברייתא is teaching that a vow on a day already forbidden by a fast still counts.
steps.deeperAnalysis: On the fast of גדליה, the person may not eat or drink anyway. So we might think his vow adds nothing, and a later vow attached to that day would just be attached to a normal prohibition, which does not work. The ברייתא teaches that his vow does take hold, so it is a real vow that can be attached to.

keyTerms.meaning: The leader whose murder is marked by a public fast
It was needed for this
You might have thought
Attached to a vow
It teaches us otherwise

steps.whatToRemember: A vow made on a day that is already forbidden still takes hold. So a person can attach a new vow to it.
steps.confusionAlert: The 'פלוני' in the ברייתא is גדליה בן אחיקם. The whole point is that his day is a public fast, which is why the case is a new teaching.

phrases.aramaic: כְּיוֹם שֶׁנֶּהֱרַג בּוֹ גְּדַלְיָה בֶּן אֲחִיקָם
phrases.english: Like the day on which גדליה בן אחיקם was killed,
it was needed for that.
It might enter your mind to say:

phrases.aramaic: כֵּיוָן דְּכִי לָא נָדַר נָמֵי אָסוּר –
phrases.english: since even if he did not vow, it is forbidden anyway,
then even when he did vow,
no prohibition of a vow takes hold on him,
and so this one is not attaching to a vow;
it teaches us that it does.

steps.triggerLanguage: כְּיוֹם שֶׁנֶּהֱרַג בּוֹ גְּדַלְיָה בֶּן אֲחִיקָם אִיצְטְרִיךְ לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the 'obvious' challenge by pointing to the second example.
steps.terutzResolutionType: The new teaching is in the second example of the ברייתא.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A vow on a day already forbidden by a fast does not take hold, so one cannot attach to it.
steps.terutzMaskana: The vow does take hold even on a fast day, so attaching to it works.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that a vow can take hold even when the thing is already forbidden for another reason.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן also holds like רבא
steps.stepSummary: רבין reports that רבי יוחנן said 'אִיסָּר, I will not eat of yours' is a שבועה. This matches רבא's view.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן also agrees with רבא. When רבין came, he reported that רבי יוחנן said: if someone says 'By a מבטא, I will not eat of yours' or 'By an אִיסָּר, I will not eat of yours', it is a שבועה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings support for רבא from a statement of רבי יוחנן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא held that the word אִיסָּר on its own creates a שבועה. רבי יוחנן rules the same way: saying מבטא or אִיסָּר together with 'I will not eat' is a full שבועה. So רבא is not alone in this view.

keyTerms.meaning: An utterance; a word used for making an oath
A bond; here it means binding oneself with an oath
An oath

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yochanan also holds
like this view of Rava;
for when Ravin came
he said that Rabbi Yochanan said:
"By an utterance, I will not eat of yours,"
"By a bond, I will not eat of yours" –
it is an oath.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאַף רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן סָבַר לַהּ לְהָא דְּרָבָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the discussion of אִיסָּר by showing that רבי יוחנן agrees with רבא.
steps.raayaObject: רבא's view that the word אִיסָּר on its own is a שבועה
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבין's report of רבי יוחנן's ruling about מבטא and אִיסָּר

steps.title: Future oaths are שקר, past oaths are שוא, and קונמות break 'לא יחל'
steps.stepSummary: רב דימי reports that רבי יוחנן divides oaths into two kinds, each with its own warning פסוק. He also gives the warning for קונמות.
steps.simpleTranslation: When רב דימי came, he reported that רבי יוחנן said: 'I will eat' or 'I will not eat' is called שקר. Its warning comes from 'Do not swear falsely by My name.' 'I ate' or 'I did not eat' is called שוא. Its warning comes from 'Do not take the name of ה׳ your God in vain.' Someone who breaks קונמות transgresses 'He shall not break his word.'
steps.whatsHappening: A new teaching begins. רבי יוחנן sorts different false oaths into categories and gives the warning from the תורה for each one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A future oath that is not kept is called שקר. A false oath about the past is called שוא. Each one has a separate לאו. Vows made with קונם (making something forbidden like a קרבן) are a separate category again, under 'לֹא יַחֵל דְּבָרוֹ'.

keyTerms.meaning: False; here, a broken oath about the future
In vain; here, a false oath about the past
A Torah warning (the לאו behind a punishment)
Vows that make an item forbidden like a קרבן
'He shall not break his word': the לאו for vows

steps.whatToRemember: According to רבי יוחנן: future oath = שקר, past oath = שוא, and קונמות = 'לֹא יַחֵל דְּבָרוֹ'.

phrases.english: When Rav Dimi came
he said that Rabbi Yochanan said:
"I will eat" or "I will not eat" – is false,
and its warning is from here:
"You shall not swear by My name falsely."
"I ate" or "I did not eat" – is in vain,
and its warning is from here:

phrases.aramaic: ״לֹא תִשָּׂא אֶת שֵׁם ה׳ אֱלֹהֶיךָ לַשָּׁוְא״.
phrases.english: "You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain."
Konamot (vows of 'like a sacrifice') –
one transgresses "he shall not break his word."

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי אֲתָא רַב דִּימִי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new teaching from רבי יוחנן, this time reported by רב דימי.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A broken future oath is שקר (warning: 'לֹא תִשָּׁבְעוּ בִשְׁמִי לַשָּׁקֶר'). A false oath about the past is שוא (warning: 'לֹא תִשָּׂא'). Breaking קונמות transgresses 'לֹא יַחֵל דְּבָרוֹ'.

steps.title: Challenge: a ברייתא says שוא and שקר are the same
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא says שוא and שקר are 'one'. That seems to mean שקר is also about the past, which goes against רבי יוחנן.
steps.simpleTranslation: The גמרא challenges this: a ברייתא teaches that שוא and שקר are one. Doesn't that mean that since שוא is about the past, שקר is also about the past? Then 'I ate' and 'I did not eat' would be called שקר!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks רבי יוחנן's rule using a ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוחנן said שוא is about the past and שקר is about the future. The ברייתא calls them 'one'. The גמרא reads this to mean they cover the same kind of oath. If so, a past oath like 'I ate' would also be שקר, which goes against רבי יוחנן's split.

keyTerms.meaning: About the past
Apparently; so it turns out

phrases.english: They raised an objection:
"In vain" and "false" are one.
What, is it not that since "in vain" is about the past –
"false" is also about the past?
Apparently, "I ate" or "I did not eat"
is a false oath!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבי יוחנן's division of oaths from step 8.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יוחנן's rule that שקר is only about the future and שוא is about the past
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא calls שוא and שקר 'one'. That suggests that just as שוא is about the past, שקר is also about the past. So 'I ate' would be שקר, which contradicts רבי יוחנן.

steps.title: The two kinds of oaths stay separate
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the challenge. שבועת שקר and שבועת שוא each keep their own definition.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is that really a problem? This one is as it is, and that one is as it is.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question from Step 9. The ברייתא's word 'one' does not erase the difference between שוא and שקר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge assumed that 'one' meant שקר must also be about the past. The גמרא says no: שוא is still about the past and שקר is still about the future, just as רבי יוחנן said. The next step explains what 'one' really means.

keyTerms.meaning: Is that really comparable? Is that a real problem? A way of pushing back on a challenge
This one is as it is, and that one is as it is. Each case keeps its own rule
An oath taken in vain (here, about the past)
A false oath (here, about the future)

phrases.english: Are the cases comparable?!
This one is as it is, and that one is as it is.
phrases.notes: 'This one' is the false oath (שקר) and 'that one' is the oath in vain (שוא).

steps.triggerLanguage: מִידֵּי אִירְיָא? הָא כִּדְאִיתָא, וְהָא כִּדְאִיתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of Step 9 against רבי יוחנן
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpreting the ברייתא's wording so it does not merge the two categories
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'One' means שקר is also about the past
steps.terutzMaskana: Each kind of oath keeps its own definition, as רבי יוחנן said

steps.title: 'One' means said in a single utterance
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא calls them 'one' because both were said by ה׳ at once, just like זכור and שמור.
steps.simpleTranslation: So what does 'they are one' mean? It means they were said in one utterance. As a ברייתא teaches: 'Remember' and 'Observe' were said in one utterance, in a way that a human mouth cannot speak and a human ear cannot hear.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains what 'one' means in the ברייתא. Both oath prohibitions were said by ה׳ at the same moment.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The 'oneness' is about how the words were spoken, not about what they mean. The גמרא brings a parallel case: זכור in שמות and שמור in דברים were also spoken together miraculously. So two different פסוקים can be 'one' in delivery and still teach different things.

keyTerms.meaning: One utterance, said together at the same moment
'Remember' the שבת day (שמות 20:8)
'Observe' the שבת day (דברים 5:12)
As a ברייתא teaches

phrases.english: And what does 'they are one thing' mean?
That they were said in one utterance,
phrases.notes: He means שוא and שקר were said by ה׳ together at one moment, the same way זכור and שמור were.

phrases.english: as it is taught in a ברייתא:
'Remember' and 'Observe' were said in one utterance,
something the mouth cannot say,
and something the ear cannot hear.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמַאי דָּבָר אֶחָד הֵן? דִּבְדִיבּוּר אֶחָד נֶאֶמְרוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the answer by explaining the ברייתא's word 'one'
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining a term: 'one' refers to the way the words were spoken
steps.terutzMaskana: 'One' means spoken in a single divine utterance

steps.title: What law does the single utterance teach here?
steps.stepSummary: For זכור and שמור, the single utterance teaches that women must say קידוש. What does it teach for oaths?
steps.simpleTranslation: It makes sense there that they were said in one utterance, because of רב אדא בר אהבה's teaching. רב אדא בר אהבה said: Women are obligated in קידוש of the day by the law of the תורה, because the תורה says 'Remember' and 'Observe.' Anyone who must observe must also remember. Since women must observe, they must also remember. But here, what law do we need it for?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer of Step 11. With זכור and שמור, saying them together teaches a real law. With oaths, what does it teach?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Linking זכור to שמור teaches that women, who must keep the שבת prohibitions, also must say קידוש. That is true even though קידוש is a time-bound מצוה. The גמרא expects the 'single utterance' of the oath פסוקים to teach some practical law too, and it asks what that law is.

keyTerms.meaning: It makes sense (there), but... It opens a contrast that leads to a question
Sanctifying the שבת day with קידוש
By Torah law
Observing (keeping the prohibitions) / remembering (saying קידוש)
For what practical law?

phrases.english: It makes sense there that they were said in one utterance,
in line with רב אדא בר אהבה,
as רב אדא בר אהבה said:
Women are obligated in sanctifying the day
by Torah law,
because the verse says 'Remember' and 'Observe':
anyone included in observing is included in remembering,
and these women, since they are included in observing,
are also included in remembering.

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא הָכָא לְמַאי הִלְכְתָא מִיבְּעֵי לֵיהּ?
phrases.english: But here, for what law is it needed?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the explanation in Step 11 by asking for its practical purpose
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that שוא and שקר are 'one' only because they were said in one utterance
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A single utterance should teach a practical law, like קידוש for women. For oaths, no such law has been named yet.

steps.title: The link teaches lashes: from שוא to שקר
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests the link teaches that just as one gets lashes for שוא, one also gets lashes for שקר.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, just as one gets lashes for an oath in vain, so too one gets lashes for a false oath.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a first suggestion for the practical law: מלקות (lashes). It compares שקר to שוא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Because the two prohibitions were said together, they share a punishment. This version treats שוא as the obvious case and uses it to teach lashes for שקר. The next step questions which direction makes sense.

keyTerms.meaning: Receives lashes (מלקות)
Just as... so too. A comparison formula

phrases.english: Rather, just as one gets lashes for an oath in vain,
so too one gets lashes for a false oath.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 12 by naming the law that the single utterance teaches
steps.terutzResolutionType: Identifying a shared punishment learned from the linkage
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The single utterance teaches nothing practical
steps.terutzMaskana: It teaches that both oaths carry lashes (Step 15 corrects which way the comparison runs)

steps.title: That is backwards!
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects that the comparison runs in the wrong direction.
steps.simpleTranslation: Isn't it the other way around?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא complains that the comparison in Step 13 is upside down. This sets up a corrected version in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Lashes for a false oath about the future are the obvious case, because a person breaks that oath through an action. An oath in vain about the past is only speech, so that is the case that needs a source. You learn the unclear case from the clear one, not the reverse.

keyTerms.meaning: Which way is it facing? Isn't it the opposite? Used when an argument is backwards

phrases.english: Isn't it the other way around?
phrases.notes: Literally 'toward which side?' The גמרא means the comparison is facing the wrong direction.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the direction of the comparison in Step 13
steps.kashyaTarget: Learning lashes for שקר from שוא
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Lashes for שקר (broken through an action) are obvious. It is lashes for שוא (only words) that need to be learned.

steps.title: Corrected: from שקר to שוא
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא flips the comparison: just as one gets lashes for שקר, one also gets lashes for שוא.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, say this: just as one gets lashes for a false oath, so too one gets lashes for an oath in vain.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא fixes the wording of the comparison. The 'one utterance' teaches that שוא also carries lashes, like שקר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now the clear case (שקר, broken with an action) teaches the unclear case (שוא, only words). This finally gives the practical law the single utterance teaches. It also keeps רבי יוחנן's two separate categories in place.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather, say it this way. It introduces a corrected version
Lashes, the punishment for breaking a לאו

steps.whatToRemember: שוא and שקר are two separate kinds of oaths, as רבי יוחנן said. They are 'one' only because ה׳ said them in a single utterance. That link teaches that an oath in vain gets lashes just like a false oath.
steps.whyThisMatters: This defends רבי יוחנן's split between past and future oaths. It also shows that the 'single utterance' idea always teaches some practical law.

phrases.english: Rather, say:
just as one gets lashes for a false oath,
so too one gets lashes for an oath in vain.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא אֵימָא כְּשֵׁם שֶׁלּוֹקֶה עַל שֶׁקֶר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the objection of Step 14 by reversing the comparison
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The single utterance teaches that one gets lashes for שבועת שוא just as for שבועת שקר. The two kinds of oaths stay separate, as רבי יוחנן said.

steps.title: Isn't it obvious that both get lashes?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the ברייתא had to teach lashes for both oaths, since both are a לאו.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is obvious! This one is a prohibition and that one is a prohibition.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the need for the teaching from Step 15. Both kinds of oath break a לאו, and someone who breaks a לאו normally gets מלקות, so why say it?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 15 used the shared utterance to teach that שבועת שוא gets lashes like שבועת שקר. The גמרא now asks whether that lesson is needed at all. Each one has its own לאו (Step 8: 'לא תשבעו בשמי לשקר' for שקר, 'לא תשא' for שוא), and a לאו normally brings מלקות, so the teaching seems to add nothing new.

keyTerms.meaning: It's obvious! The גמרא's way of asking why something needed to be said
A negative commandment, a 'do not'
Lashes, the usual punishment for breaking a לאו

phrases.english: It is obvious! This one is a prohibition and that one is a prohibition!
phrases.notes: Each oath has its own לאו (see step 8), and a לאו normally means lashes.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges whether the conclusion of Step 15 is needed at all
steps.kashyaTarget: The need to teach that both שבועת שקר and שבועת שוא get lashes
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Every לאו normally brings מלקות, and both oaths are a לאו, so the teaching seems to add nothing new.

steps.title: You might have thought 'לא ינקה' means no cleansing at all
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא begins its answer. Without the teaching, we might have read 'לא ינקה' the way רב פפא did, as 'never cleansed at all'.
steps.simpleTranslation: You might have said, as רב פפא said to אביי, that 'He will not be cleared' means not at all.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts to explain why the teaching is not obvious. It brings up רב פפא's reading of the פסוק. This step sets up the rest of the answer, which continues on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'מהו דתימא' signals that the teaching is needed to rule out a mistaken idea. That idea comes from רב פפא: the words 'לא ינקה' could mean a person who takes ה׳'s name in vain is never cleared of his sin, even if he is punished. The גמרא will now explain how that idea might have made this oath different from a normal לאו.

keyTerms.meaning: You might have said. It introduces a mistaken idea that the teaching comes to rule out
He will not be cleared of guilt, from the פסוק about taking ה׳'s name in vain
At all

steps.confusionAlert: The answer is not finished on this amud. The גמרא only gives the starting point, רב פפא's reading. How that reading connects to lashes continues on the next amud.

phrases.english: You might have said
as Rav Pappa said to Abaye:
'He will not be cleared' means not at all;

steps.triggerLanguage: מַהוּ דְּתֵימָא כְּדַאֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב פָּפָּא לְאַבָּיֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins answering the פשיטא challenge of Step 16
steps.terutzResolutionType: מהו דתימא: the teaching is needed to rule out a mistaken reading
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Based on רב פפא's reading of 'לא ינקה' as 'not at all', one might have thought this oath works differently from a normal לאו. The answer continues in the next lines.
steps.terutzMaskana: Still in progress. The teaching is needed to rule out the conclusion one might draw from 'לא ינקה'.
